There are three things people confuse, and confusing them is how a note becomes evidence against the company rather than for it. An allegation is what somebody claims. Hearsay is what somebody was told by a third person and did not witness. A finding is what you concluded and can support. Keep them in separate paragraphs and label them, because in eighteen months nobody will remember which was which and the document will be read by a lawyer, not by you. Second point. Report what was said, do not interpret it. He said he had not been told the deadline is a sentence I can defend. He clearly did not care about the deadline is a sentence that will cost us. And the last one, which people hate. If a point was not substantiated, write that it was not substantiated. A note that substantiates everything is a note nobody believes.

When I take one of these to the executive team, I have two minutes and three people who described the same afternoon differently. What I used to do was tell it chronologically, and by minute two nobody could hold three timelines in their head. What I do now is start with what is not in dispute. All three agree that the meeting happened on the fourteenth and that it lasted about forty minutes. That takes fifteen seconds and it steadies the room. Then I say where they diverge, in one sentence each. He said he had raised it twice. She said she had no record of either conversation. The third person told us she was not in the room. And then, only then, what I concluded and what I could not. If you start with the disagreement, everybody picks a side before they have the facts, and you spend the rest of the meeting arguing with people who chose in the first ten seconds.
